Package frc.robot.aiming

Class LeadCompensator

java.lang.Object
frc.robot.aiming.LeadCompensator
public class LeadCompensator extends Object
Computes a lead-compensated virtual target position so the shooter accounts for robot motion during ball flight.

The Problem

A ball fired from a moving robot takes roughly 0.3â€“0.8 seconds to reach the hub. During that time the robot keeps moving. If we aim directly at the hub from our current position, the ball will miss because the shooter has moved by the time the ball arrives.

The Solution: Virtual Target

Instead of aiming at the real hub, we aim at a virtual target â€” a point shifted backward by fieldVelocity Ã— tof. When the ball is launched toward this virtual target the ball's path in field coordinates still passes through the real hub at arrival time, because the robot's motion adds to the ball's field-frame velocity.

Mathematically, the required field-frame launch angle is: 

   Î¸ = atan2(hub - (robotPos + velocity Ã— tof))
     = atan2(virtualTarget - robotPos)
where virtualTarget = hub - velocity Ã— tof.

Why Iterate?

The tof depends on distance to the virtual target (looked up from measured data), but the virtual target position depends on tof. We iterate to find the fixed point:
  1. Use the current best virtual target to ask the inner aim strategy for tof.
  2. Shift the real hub by -velocity Ã— tof to get a new virtual target.
  3. Repeat until the virtual target stops moving ({'@literal <}1 mm change).
In practice, convergence takes 3â€“4 iterations even at top FRC drive speeds (~5 m/s).

Why kZero Velocity to the Inner Strategy?

The inner strategy (ToFAim) also has its own internal lead-compensation loop that shifts the shooter position by velocity Ã— tof. If we passed the real velocity here, lead would be applied twice â€” once by this class (virtual target shift) and once by ToFAim internally. Passing Translation2d.kZero tells ToFAim "treat the robot as stationary" so it only solves for pitch/speed/tof from the static virtual target, and we own the lead.

Relationship to ToFAim

Both approaches are mathematically equivalent and produce the same final yaw angle. The advantage of this class is that it stores the converged virtual target as an intermediate value, making the lead offset observable for telemetry (Aiming/LeadOffsetXM, Aiming/LeadOffsetYM in SmartDashboard).

      public static edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Pose3d computeLeadTarget(edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Pose3d hubPose, edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Pose3d shooterPose, edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Translation2d fieldVelocity, AimStrategy strategy)
      Returns the converged virtual target pose that accounts for the robot's field velocity.

      The returned pose is the hub position shifted by -fieldVelocity Ã— tof at convergence. When the robot is stationary, this equals hubPose exactly. When moving, it shifts "behind" the hub in the direction of travel by roughly speed Ã— tof meters (typically 0.3â€“1.5 m at competition speeds).

      After calling this method, pass the returned pose to the inner aim strategy with Translation2d.kZero velocity to get final pitch/speed/yaw without double-counting the lead: 

         Pose3d lead = LeadCompensator.computeLeadTarget(hub, shooter, vel, m_tofAim);
   AimParams params = m_tofAim.update(lead, shooter, Translation2d.kZero);
      Parameters:
      hubPose - true hub position on the field (from the AprilTag layout)
      shooterPose - current shooter pose in field coordinates
      fieldVelocity - robot field-relative velocity in m/s; typically from ChassisSpeeds.fromRobotRelativeSpeeds(...)
      strategy - inner aim strategy â€” called with Translation2d.kZero velocity so it computes pitch/speed/tof for a static virtual target
      Returns:
      converged virtual target; equals hubPose when stationary or when the inner strategy returns Impossible
